source.title: Control questions matter: introspection, refusal ablation, and gates in open Gemma models

record.tranche_reason: The post applies refusal-direction ablation while investigating introspection, but reports introspection and control-question outcomes rather than testing refusal behaviour, capability retention, or any other listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The post tests how refusal-direction ablation affects introspection under concept-vector injection. Those are related outcomes, but not the refusal behaviour named in the versions, so the ablation results are recorded under fits_no_version. The reported prompt-variant introspection rates and gate/carrier findings are not results about the refusal direction or the listed claim versions. The cited +53% result from another work is not recorded as this study's result.
record.test_reason: The post uses refusal-direction ablation, both a supplied abliterated Gemma 3 checkpoint and last-token-only ablation, as a tool inside concept-vector introspection experiments. It reports introspection and control-question Yes−No logit shifts. It never measures refusal rates, induced refusal, or capability retention under ablation alone. So it does not test any version of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The author concludes that the cited +53% detection gain from refusal ablation does not survive a control question run under injection. Full-token abliteration plus injection causes severe confusion, while last-token-only ablation gives a small, clean improvement.
record.recipe_differences: The post applies refusal-direction ablation in an introspection experiment using concept-vector injection, including a supplied abliterated checkpoint and last-token-only ablations. It does not report the claimed refusal-behaviour tests.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports that the outcome depends on whether ablation is applied to the abliterated model or only at the last user token; it also notes that injection changes the control-question result.

fits_no_version.finding: Under concept-vector injection, the supplied Gemma 3 abliterated model shows +6.64 introspection logits and +32.31 control-question (1+1=3) logits. The two logit differences become nearly identical, which the author reads as severe confusion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Full-token refusal abliteration combined with activation injection produces large degradation on unrelated Yes/No control questions. This confounds apparent introspection gains.

fits_no_version.finding: Last-token-only refusal-direction ablation during injection gives small introspection gains with small control shifts: Gemma 3 27b +0.307/+0.662, Gemma 2 9b +1.126/+0.527.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Position-restricted refusal-direction ablation slightly raises injected-concept detection with little control-question disruption.

record.problems: The post reports no uncertainty estimates for the ablation results. The supplied abliterated-model comparison is described as showing near-identical logits, but the figure's numerical values are not present in the text. The evidence concerns introspection and one arithmetic control question, not refusal rates or broad capability.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows from the refusal-ablation section were left out. Other prompt-variant rates and gate/carrier results were omitted because they do not report outcomes of the refusal direction or test a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Whether ablating the direction removes refusal, whether adding it induces refusal, and whether other abilities are kept without concept injection.
Whether the abliterated weight edit removes refusal. The supplied checkpoint is used only for introspection tests under injection.
Jailbreak mechanism and adversarial training against ablation.
Whether refusal has a multi-direction, affine or cone structure.
Whether harmfulness and refusal are encoded separately.
Transfer across languages or models. Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 directions are applied separately, but transfer is not tested.
Whether training determines that a removable direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: The control-question degradation of the abliterated model (r2, r7, and raw answers such as '! ! ! !' for 1+1=3) touches V1/V2's 'other abilities largely kept'. However, it appears only when ablation is combined with concept-vector injection. The author notes the degradation is absent in no-injection false-positive checks. It is therefore not a clean capability test of ablation, and I gave no V1/V2 label. The prompt variant for the last-token table rows is not stated; the accompanying plots use the short prompt. The +53% figure is a cited result from Macar et al. and is correctly excluded from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: Refusal removal, induced refusal, and preservation of other capabilities.
Whether a weight edit removes refusal in released models.
Whether attacks suppress the direction or training against ablation improves robustness.
Whether refusal is represented by an affine structure, cone, or multiple directions.
Whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from refusal.
Transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Whether refusal training determines the existence of a removable direction.
Whether the claim holds for reasoning models.

relation.reason: Ablation is applied to study introspection. Refusal behaviour is never measured.

tranche.reason: The post uses refusal-direction ablation (the supplied abliterated checkpoint and last-token ablation) as a tool in concept-injection introspection experiments. It reports only introspection and control-question logit shifts and gives no refusal rates, so it does not test any version.

source_check.notes: The authors_conclusion paraphrase is correct. In the abliterated (all-token) model under injection, the control logit shift is +32.31 against +6.64 for introspection. This is a coherence cost of abliteration, but it appears only together with concept injection, so it is at most context for V2 side effects and not a refusal test. The +53% figure is the cited paper's result, not this post's. The source is an informal single-author post with thesis highlights.
